projects.title: Movah
projects.summary: A mobile app to keep track of series, films and anime without losing the thread. Flutter on Android and iOS, with Supabase.
projects.lead: A mobile app to keep track of series, films and anime without losing the thread. Flutter on Android and iOS, with Supabase.

context: With so many streaming platforms, it is easy to forget where you are in a series or when the next episode comes out. Movah brings together what you are watching, what you want to watch and what is coming soon.
A personal project, taken from mockup to app, to see a complete mobile product through: accounts, data, sync and release on two platforms.
work: I designed the high-fidelity mockup, then built the Flutter app and its Supabase backend.
workList: Tracking series, films and anime, episode by episode.
The catalogue and search, powered by the TMDB API.
The upcoming release calendar, lists and statistics.
Sign-in with email, Google or Apple, in French and English.
choices: The app never calls TMDB directly: Supabase Edge Functions sit in between, with a cache in Postgres. The API key stays on the server, and screens keep showing the last known data if TMDB does not respond.
The code is organised by feature, in data, domain and presentation layers. Domain entities depend on neither Flutter nor Supabase, which keeps them easy to test; app state goes through Riverpod.
result: The app runs on Android and iOS, with light and dark themes true to the mockup.
Every change goes through GitHub Actions continuous integration: formatting, code analysis, tests, then the app build.
lessons: Starting from a complete mockup before writing the first line saved a lot of back-and-forth: every screen already had its states, colours and copy.
Moving from Angular to Flutter showed me that the same ideas carry over between frameworks: small components and data that flows in one direction.
captions: Following a series, episode by episode.

projects.title: RDI Manager
projects.summary: R&D activity tracking at Object as a Service: time, planning, metrics. I took over maintenance and modernised the Symfony and Vue.js application.
projects.lead: R&D activity tracking at Object as a Service: time, planning, metrics. Symfony back end, Vue.js interface.

context: RDI Manager is the internal tool that tracks R&D activity at Object as a Service: time spent on each project, the team's schedule and the metrics used to follow research projects.
The application pairs a Symfony back end with a Vue.js interface. It had been running for years on an old Symfony version. Every change took longer, and nobody dared touch the metrics calculation.
work: I took over maintenance of the tool, then its modernisation, without interrupting the team using it.
workList: Upgrading PHP, Symfony and dependencies, step by step.
Tests on the metrics calculation before any change.
Rewriting the most fragile parts: time entry and calculations.
Fixes and features requested by the R&D team, on both the Symfony and Vue.js sides.
choices: A full rewrite would have frozen the tool for months. I chose a gradual migration: each step left the application usable, and tests checked that metrics stayed identical before and after.
The trade-off: a few older parts still live alongside the modernised code. They are isolated behind clear, documented interfaces so they can be replaced later.
result: The tool runs on a maintained Symfony version, and changes no longer risk breaking the metrics calculation.
The R&D team kept entering time and following its projects throughout the modernisation.
lessons: Starting with tests was the best investment of the project: without them, every upgrade would have been a gamble.
Taking over someone else's code taught me to read before judging. Several oddities had a business reason that needed understanding before fixing them.

projects.title: Kodoka CRM
projects.summary: A custom CRM for Kodoka: interfaces, business rules and data management.
projects.lead: A custom CRM for Kodoka: interfaces, business rules and data management.

context: Kodoka tracked its clients and sales conversations in separate files. Information was scattered and hard to share across the team.
The company wanted a simple CRM that fit the way it works, rather than a general-purpose tool that takes weeks to configure.
work: In two months, I designed and built the CRM with CodeIgniter 4, from the database to the screens.
workList: Client and contact records, with the history of exchanges.
Tracking sales opportunities, stage by stage.
Business rules: statuses, follow-ups and role-based permissions.
Importing existing data from the old files.
choices: CodeIgniter 4 was lightweight and already known to the team who would take the tool over after me. For a two-month project, that mattered more than a fuller framework.
I kept a plain, server-rendered interface to deliver on time. Only the most used screens got a little JavaScript, to avoid page reloads.
result: The team finds clients, their contacts and the history of exchanges in one place, instead of separate files.
The code was handed over with setup and onboarding documentation, so the team could keep developing it.
lessons: I would have spent more time with users before modelling the data: two fields added at the end of the project would have been obvious after a morning of observation.
Delivering a whole project in two months taught me to split work into usable versions, rather than finishing everything at once.

projects.title: IOTPlatform
projects.summary: Monitoring and control of LoRaWAN sensors for Object as a Service. Angular and NgRx front end, improvements to the Django back end.
projects.lead: Monitoring and control of LoRaWAN sensors and actuators, published by Object as a Service. I built the Angular front end and improved the Django back end.

context: IOTPlatform lets industrial operators, network managers and local authorities monitor and control their equipment remotely: level, flow or temperature sensors, and actuators, on the Orange LoRa and The Things Network networks.
The platform collects and decodes the frames sent by devices, triggers alerts by email or SMS, and sends commands to actuators.
work: I owned the whole Angular front end: designing pages and components, API calls and state management with NgRx.
On the Django back end, I improved the existing code and added several features.
workList: Sending commands to actuators, with their history.
Time-series charts and CSV data export.
choices: Data comes from many devices and changes often. I centralised application state with NgRx: screens read the same store, API calls go through effects, and updated data is updated everywhere at once.
I split the interface into reusable components (tables, charts, forms) shared between screens. The interface stays consistent as features are added.
result: The Angular front end is the clients' entry point for monitoring, commands and alerts.
lessons: Working on a live product taught me to evolve existing code without breaking what clients use every day.
NgRx takes more code up front, but it keeps application behaviour predictable as screens multiply.
captions: Sending a command to an actuator.
